title: Clean Slates: Debts Unmade by Decree
eyes: The Constitution of the Athenians (Aristotle's school)
Athenian jurors' oath and the Common Peace of 338/7 BC
The synod of Egyptian priests at Memphis (Rosetta decree)
Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, Cleopatra II and Cleopatra III (amnesty decrees, P.Tebt. 5)
places: Alexandria (issuing court); copy at Kerkeosiris in the Fayum
Athens; afterwards ten years of travel, including Egypt
Babylon; stele copies set up in temple cities (the surviving stele was carried off to Susa in antiquity)
Babylon; the copies come from northern Babylonia (Sippar)
Memphis; one copy of the stela was later reused at Rashid (Rosetta) in the Delta
intro: For about seventeen centuries, rulers and assemblies across the ancient Near East and the Greek world sometimes decided that certain debts would cease to exist. The Babylonian name for the act was misharum, 'justice' or 'making straight'; its companion andurārum meant release, a return to a former state. Hebrew had the cognate deror, 'liberty', and Athens had the seisachtheia, the 'shaking-off of burdens'. Each assumes that a debt is not a fact of nature but an agreement held in common, recorded on clay, stone or papyrus, and that a community, or the person speaking for it, can unmake it. The record here is not made of diaries. For Babylon it is royal year-names, a law stele and the damaged copies of Ammi-saduqa's edict, which survive in Istanbul and the British Museum. For Judah it is the first-person memoir of the governor Nehemiah and the edited Book of Jeremiah. For Athens it is Solon's own defensive poems, which survive only because the Constitution of the Athenians and Plutarch quoted them centuries later. For Egypt it is the priests' decree on the Rosetta Stone and a village scribe's copy of an amnesty. Every entry is tagged honestly as firsthand, later firsthand, secondhand, official record or legend. Most of the eyes are institutions, a chancery, a synod or a jurors' oath, not private people. The question that runs through every record is who decided. Babylonian kings decreed releases, often at accession, and their scribes wrote in the loopholes creditors would try and the penalties for trying. Merchants' partnership capital was protected and chattel slaves were left unfreed. Nehemiah, a Persian appointee, shamed his own class in an assembly and bound them by oath. Solon was given full power by both sides and disappointed both. Fourth-century Athens then had its jurors swear never to allow another cancellation, and Plato listed the demand among a tyrant's tricks. The Ptolemies forgave only debts owed to the crown, after revolts, in decrees the temples carved for them. Scholars disagree about what these acts were, and the chapter sets out the positions without choosing between them. One view, argued by Michael Hudson among others, sees a long Near Eastern tradition of periodic restoration: rituals of renewal that kept a free farming population from sliding into bondage, which the biblical seventh-year and Jubilee laws (Deuteronomy 15, Leviticus 25) turned into a fixed cycle. Others stress that the Babylonian decrees came irregularly. They clustered at accessions but also fell mid-reign: Ammi-ditana's appears to date to his 21st year. On this view they were political instruments for winning loyalty or easing a crisis, and having to repeat them showed the system was never fixed. The biblical laws are undated legal texts. Whether a Jubilee was ever kept is itself debated, so they appear here only as context. Ancient writers argued in the same way: Plutarch records that Androtion thought Solon had only lowered interest. Gaps. No Old Babylonia

title: The Dream Books: Nights Written Down as Evidence
places: Court, during the summer of plague and Parliament
Cyrene and his estates in Libya
His house at Mortlake on the Thames; Bohemia and Bremen 1583–89
Kōzanji, Toganoo; earlier hermitages in Kii province
The Asclepieion of Pergamum (145–147) and his estates and Smyrna afterwards
The Hague, Delft, Amsterdam, then London
The Navy Office in Seething Lane and, in the plague, Greenwich
Winter quarters on the Danube (Neuburg or near Ulm, as later accounts say)
intro: An old Chinese text, the Zhuangzi, tells of a man who dreamed he was a butterfly and on waking could not be sure whether he was a man who had dreamed of a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming it was a man. The passage has no date and no diarist, so it stands here only as a question. The people in this chapter did something more practical with the same uncertainty: they wrote their dreams down, with dates, and treated them as evidence about the waking world, then checked what happened next. The record is uneven, and the forms are named honestly. Aelius Aristides, a sick Greek orator, kept dream notes during his years with Asclepius and later built them into the Sacred Tales. Myōe, a Japanese monk, kept loose dream sheets for forty years, some now in museums. John Dee, Archbishop Laud and Samuel Pepys wrote dreams into diaries beside their daily business. Cardano and Aristides wrote theirs up long afterwards. Descartes's dreams survive only through a biographer's paraphrase and two lines in Leibniz's handwriting. Asiye Hatun of Skopje wrote her dreams as letters to her Sufi sheikh. Swedenborg's pocket journal of 1743–44 is the last and the most continuous. What joins them is the test. Aristides obeyed a dream and recorded the result on his body. Myōe took a dream as the gods' acceptance of a postponed ceremony. Cardano rewrote a prescription after a dream. Dee prayed to confirm a neighbour's dream. Descartes, a year after his night of dreams, noted that he had begun to understand what it promised. Laud wrote that he was not moved by dreams and kept recording them anyway. Swedenborg asked whether the figure in his vision was really Christ. The record ledger shows the gaps between dream and telling: hours for Myōe, Dee, Pepys and Swedenborg; decades for Aristides and Cardano; seventy years and another man's pen for Descartes. Several dreams reached print only because someone else chose to print them, a rival prosecutor in Laud's case and a librarian in Swedenborg's. Gaps: no dated dream entry by Fujiwara no Teika is included, and the Mughal emperor Jahangir's memoirs, which report dreams other people sent him about his accession, are not used as an eye. Most non-European records here survive only in modern translations, so they are summarised rather than quoted. Synesius' treatise On Dreams (c. 404) is included as context: it is the text that tells readers to keep a dream book, not a dream book itself.

title: The Shadow of the Living Light
eyes: Hartwig of Stade, Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen
places: Clairvaux, Champagne; at Trier with the pope in winter 1147–48 (per the Vita)
Disibodenberg and Rupertsberg, then Bassum near Bremen
Disibodenberg on the Nahe, then the Rupertsberg opposite Bingen
intro: In 1141 a forty-two-year-old nun in a monastery on the Nahe saw, by her own later account, a fiery light pour into her mind and heard a command to write. For a decade she wrote, slowly and privately, with one monk and one young nun as witnesses. Then she did something unusual for a visionary: before letting the book go out, she sent it upward, first in a letter to Bernard of Clairvaux, then through her abbot and the archbishop of Mainz, until, by her biographers' account, Pope Eugenius III read from it aloud at a synod in Trier in the winter of 1147–48. This chapter's record is not a diary. It is a preface written into the book itself, a run of dated letters, a memoir Hildegard dictated in old age that survives inside her saint's life, and that saint's life itself, the Vita, begun by Gottfried around 1174 and finished by Theoderich of Echternach after her death. Each entry is labelled for what it is. The most famous scene, the pope reading Scivias at Trier, is known only from the Vita, and papal letters to her come down through collections that were revised and rearranged after she died, above all the great Riesenkodex in Wiesbaden. Around Hildegard stand the people who checked, used, doubted or lost something to the new prophet: Bernard's cautious reply; Abbot Kuno, who passed her writings upward and then tried to stop her leaving; a Paris master and a neighbouring abbess who wrote with questions within months of Trier; Richardis von Stade, the nun who helped write the book and then left to be an abbess, and her brother Archbishop Hartwig, who wrote the letter reporting her death; and Elisabeth of Schönau, a younger visionary who came to Hildegard after her own public prophecies had failed. There are gaps. Richardis left no words that survive, and her wishes reach us only through people who wanted her back or wanted her gone. Kuno's side of the move is told by Hildegard's biographers. Volmar, the scribe, appears in his own voice only in one late letter whose companion reply is questioned. The illuminated Rupertsberg Scivias, whose pictures are reproduced everywhere, vanished from Dresden in 1945. A coda jumps to 1175, when a monk of Gembloux, Guibert, asked her directly how she saw. Her answer, that the light came while she was awake and never in sleep, dream or madness, is the fullest firsthand description of the experience. In 1913 and 1917 the physician-historian Charles Singer read those words and the manuscript pictures as signs of migraine aura. That reading appears here as a modern position, not a verdict, alongside her own.

title: The Missing Days
eyes: Ana de San Bartolomé (Ana García Manzanas)
Parish register of St Petri, Ystad (keeper not named)
Philip Dormer Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom) of the RSFSR
places: Alba de Tormes, Salamanca, at Teresa's bedside
Bordeaux and his château in Périgord
Rome; the bull was given at Tusculum (Frascati)
Touring southern Ireland: Cork, Waterford, Wexford, Dublin
intro: On the night of 4 October 1582 Teresa of Ávila died at Alba de Tormes, and the next morning in Catholic Spain was 15 October. A papal bull had removed ten days to bring the calendar back into line with the sun and with Easter. Over the next 336 years, country after country made the same change. Each time a whole society agreed to call tomorrow by a date eleven or thirteen days later. This chapter is built mostly from official records, letters, almanacs and a few diaries, and the form tags say so. Its core is the record of what ordinary writers did on the switch day. In September 1752 the Massachusetts parson Ebenezer Parkman and John Wesley, riding through Ireland, simply skipped from the 2nd to the 14th. Wesley added one bracketed remark. Parkman noticed that the season seemed further on than the date and kept his birthday by the old reckoning. Bunin in Moscow in 1918 called the new date 'theirs' and kept his own. Around them stand the people who made the change and the people who explained it. Gregory XIII decreed it. John Dee proposed a Protestant version in 1583, which the English bishops refused because it came from Rome. Chesterfield carried the British bill in 1751 and admitted to his son that he had not understood the astronomy. Franklin printed it for the colonies, Fukuzawa explained Japan's change in a pamphlet, and Ōkuma, years later, gave the budget reason. Montaigne wrote the first and best reflection: the calendar moved, the fields did not. A parish register in Ystad records a wedding on 30 February 1712, the one year Sweden had that day. Two stories are tested against the record. The 'calendar riots' of 1752, with crowds crying 'Give us our eleven days', have no contemporary report behind them. Robert Poole traced the story to a placard in Hogarth's satire of the 1754 Oxfordshire election, later repeated as fact; it is entered here as legend. Japan's motive is the other case. Foreigners were told the change was modernisation, while Ōkuma later recalled that it spared the government a thirteenth month of salaries. Both reasons are recorded, each labelled by who gave it and when. There are gaps. Teresa left no account of her last days; Ana de San Bartolomé's memory of them was written decades later. No firsthand record was found here of a Protestant German town's refusal of 1583–84, such as Strasbourg or the Augsburg calendar dispute. No diary of Ernest Satow or any other foreign resident in Japan was confirmed to mention the switch. Petrograd diaries of February 1918 by Zinaida Gippius and Alexander Blok were not found to mention the calendar. The eye for the Bolshevik decree is therefore an institution, not a person. The Earl of Macclesfield, who supplied the science in 1751, appears only through Chesterfield's letter.

title: With Shut Eyes: The Haunted Summer at Lake Geneva
places: Hôtel d'Angleterre, Sécheron, then Villa Diodati, Cologny
Maison Chapuis below Diodati; the lake tour 23 June–1 July; Chamonix 21–27 July
Maison Chapuis, Montalègre; Villa Diodati in the evenings; Chamonix in July
Maison Chapuis; Villa Diodati, where she copied Byron's manuscripts
Observing station in the old botanical garden, Bastion St-Léger, Geneva
Off Meillerie / St Gingolph, Lake Geneva
Villa Diodati or Maison Chapuis (her account does not say which)
Villa Diodati, Cologny; the lake tour with Shelley; the Bernese Oberland in September
Villa Diodati, late August; the Alps in September
intro: In May 1816 two groups of English exiles arrived at the same hotel at Sécheron on Lake Geneva: Lord Byron with his young physician John Polidori, and Percy Shelley with Mary Godwin, their baby son and Mary's stepsister Claire Clairmont, who was pursuing Byron. By June Byron had taken the Villa Diodati on the hill at Cologny and the Shelleys a small house below it. The weather was dreadful. The year after the eruption of Tambora, Geneva's instruments recorded a summer several degrees colder than normal, with rain on far more days than usual and not one clear day in June. Shut in by the rain, the friends read German ghost stories in French translation, talked late about the nature of life, and agreed to write ghost stories of their own. Byron began one and dropped it; Polidori's became The Vampyre (1819); Mary's became Frankenstein (1818). Monk Lewis, the most famous Gothic writer of the day, came in August and told tales of his own. This chapter sets the records of that summer side by side, and they are uneven. The only day-by-day diary is Polidori's, and he stopped writing it daily on 30 June. Mary's journal for the ghost-story weeks is lost: for those weeks there is no surviving firsthand account by her, and the famous account of her waking vision was written in 1831, fifteen years later. Claire Clairmont's journal for 1816 does not survive either, and Lewis left no record of his visit. Much of what remains is dated letters, a preface, a poem, a dated fragment, and weather registers. The record ledger therefore matters as much as the entries. It shows, for each event, when it was first written down: on the same night (Polidori on the Christabel scene), within weeks (Shelley's letter about nearly drowning), a year later (Percy's preface), three years later (the anonymous Geneva letter of 1819), or fifteen years later (Mary's Introduction). Even the night of the vision is a matter of argument: an astronomical study of 2011 placed it in the small hours of 16 June, when moonlight could have come through her shutters, while another chronology puts it about 22 June. Beside the friends stand voices from outside the circle: Marc-Auguste Pictet's Geneva weather register and Heinrich Zschokke's weather diary in Aarau, which show the cold summer was real and nationwide; and, in London, Fanny Imlay's letters and William Godwin's diary, which record the cost of the summer when the travellers came home.

title: Like Confessing a Murder: Darwin's Private Theory
places: England, writing to his London publisher Edward Moxon
London (Great Marlborough Street, then Upper Gower Street), Maer and Shrewsbury on family visits, Down House from 1842
Maer Hall, Staffordshire, then London and Down
intro: In July 1837, less than a year after the Beagle docked, Charles Darwin opened a small notebook and began to think about the 'transmutation of species'. Within fifteen months he had the mechanism, scrawled in Notebook D on 28 September 1838 after reading Malthus. He did not publish it for twenty years. This chapter covers the first seven of them, from the notebooks to the essay of 1844 and the storm over Vestiges in 1845, when the idea lived on paper in one study and in a handful of letters. The record is mostly private notebooks, a terse pocket journal, two marriage memoranda and dated letters, not diaries. The notebooks were printed only in the twentieth century; Darwin cut pages from them for later use. Laid beside them are the letters of the very few people he told: Emma Wedgwood, who heard of his religious doubts before their marriage; Joseph Hooker, a young botanist he barely knew, who received the confession 'like confessing a murder' in January 1844; and Leonard Jenyns, a clergyman friend told the same autumn. Around this inner circle stand people who were named but not told. In July 1844 Darwin ranked possible editors for his essay should he die: Lyell first, Henslow with question marks, Hooker added in the margin. No letter of this period shows Lyell or Henslow responding to the theory, and Jenyns's reply is lost; those gaps are marked on their eyes. Darwin's father, who advised him to hide his doubts, is known only from his son's memory forty years later. In October 1844 an anonymous book, Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, said in public much of what Darwin believed in private. Its author, the Edinburgh publisher Robert Chambers, was hiding a name as carefully as Darwin was hiding a theory, with letters routed through Alexander Ireland in Manchester. Darwin and Hooker read it in parallel; Adam Sedgwick, Darwin's old geology teacher, answered it with fury; Tennyson sent for it eagerly; and a young collector in Wales, Alfred Russel Wallace, decided it was a hypothesis worth testing. Read together, the records show what secrecy protected and what it cost. It gave Darwin time to accumulate facts and rehearse objections, and the Vestiges uproar showed him exactly which arguments he would face. It also left the theory dependent on one fair copy, one letter to his wife and a few correspondents, and it set up the scramble of 1858, told in Volume IV.

title: Our Hearts Are the Same: The Hidden Christians of Urakami
places: Kyoto and Osaka; Nagasaki in July 1868; abroad 1871–73
Osaka and Kyoto, spring and summer 1868
Tateyama office of the Nagasaki magistrate
Urakami village, north of Nagasaki; at Ōura church on 17 March 1865
Urakami; Nagasaki magistrate's prison; exile in western Japan
Yedo and Yokohama; met the Nagasaki governors in 1867
Ōura church on the hill above the Nagasaki foreign settlement
intro: For about 250 years after Christianity was banned in 1614, families in the villages around Nagasaki, in Urakami, Sotome and the Gotō islands, kept a faith that the state believed it had destroyed. They were registered at Buddhist temples, stepped on Christian images when the magistrate's officers came round each year, and kept their prayers, baptisms and a church calendar in the hands of their own lay leaders. Their survival depended on one condition: that nobody outside knew for certain. On 17 March 1865 a group from Urakami walked into the new French church at Ōura and broke that condition on purpose. What followed was the last great persecution of Christians in Japan. The refusal of Buddhist funerals in 1867 exposed the village; the shogun's magistrate raided its secret chapels; the new Meiji government renewed the ban and, between 1868 and 1870, scattered about 3,400 Urakami Christians among some twenty domains, where about 600 died. Western diplomats protested, the Iwakura Mission met the issue in America and Europe, and in February 1873 the notice boards banning Christianity came down. The exiles returned. The honest record is lopsided. No diary by a villager from these years has been found. The villagers' only firsthand written voice here is Takagi Sen'emon's memorandum, written later and known through modern study; the woman who spoke first at Ōura survives only in a priest's letter and church memory. Almost everything else was written by people outside the community: the French missionary to whom they disclosed themselves, the magistrates who interrogated them, the Japanese ministers who exiled them, and the British and American diplomats who argued about them. Most of these sources are letters, dispatches, protocols and decrees rather than diaries, and they are tagged that way. Read together, they show the same act described in incompatible terms. To Petitjean it was a resurrection; to the magistrate, a crime; to Sanjō Sanetomi, insubordination; to Parkes, persecution of people who shared his faith; to a Japanese official memorandum, a peaceful removal in which no one was arrested. The figures move too: 63, 65 or 68 arrested; 4,010 sentenced; Satow's 'some four thousand'; 3,394 exiled; 2,800 reported to Parliament; 613 or more dead. The chapter ends with a group the diplomats never wrote about: the hidden Christians who did not join the Church when it became legal. For them, concealment had stopped being only a disguise and had become a tradition of its own. Their practices are described here only in outline.

title: Waking Ideas: The Night and the Telling
eyes: Friedrich August Kekulé (from 1895 Kekulé von Stradonitz)
places: Budapest (1881–82), Paris and Strasbourg (1882–84), New York (from 1884)
Ghent, by the fire in his study
London; Heidelberg; Ghent; Bonn; Berlin for the 1890 celebration
On a London omnibus, riding home to Clapham
intro: Between 1858 and 1921 several of the best-known ideas in science and engineering acquired a second history: a story of how they arrived, in a reverie on a bus, by a fire, in a sunset walk, in sleep. This chapter sets those stories beside the dated documents of the same discoveries, so that the reader can see, entry by entry, when each idea was first written down and when its origin story was first told. The record ledger is the heart of the chapter. Kekulé's chains and ring were in print in 1858 and 1865; his dreams first appear in a speech of 1890. Tesla's motor is on record in a patent application of 1887 and a lecture of 1888; the walk in Budapest's City Park first appears in a magazine memoir of 1919. Loewi's frog-heart experiment was published in 1921; his double dream comes from his own writings of the 1950s, and even its year shifted in retelling. Ramanujan's letters of 1913 survive, and they never mention the goddess Namagiri, whose part in his work reaches us through family and later biographers. Around these principals stand the rivals and the record-keepers. Archibald Scott Couper reached Kekulé's theory weeks later and vanished from science; Josef Loschmidt printed ring formulas in 1861 that Kekulé dismissed; Richard Anschütz, Kekulé's student, restored both rivals and also preserved his teacher's dream speech; in 1984 John Wotiz and Susanna Rudofsky asked whether the dreams were invented, and others answered them. G. H. Hardy, the reader of Ramanujan's letters, stands as the skeptic of the mystical story, and S. R. Ranganathan as one of its first chroniclers. Two famous dream stories are included as labelled controls. Mendeleev's periodic table has a dated manuscript and a dream supplied by a colleague's later anecdote. Elias Howe's needle dream has a real patent behind it and no known source at all. Tesla's companion in the park, Antal Szigeti, is given a place though he left no account: he is the witness whose silence shows how much rests on one man's memory. Most of the record here is not diary. It is journal papers, patents, letters, a commemorative speech, a serial memoir, obituaries and biographies, each tagged with what it is and whether it is firsthand, later firsthand, secondhand or legend. Modern translations and works still in copyright are summarised; quotations come only from texts printed before 1929, including the 1890 German speech and Tesla's 1919 memoir.

title: When Money Stopped Being Believed
places: Paris; trips into Germany, including Strasbourg to Kehl across the Rhine, summer 1922
Weißenburger Straße, Prenzlauer Berg, a working-class district of north Berlin
intro: In July 1914 a dollar bought 4.20 marks. On 20 November 1923 it bought 4.2 trillion, and on that day the German authorities stopped the fall by declaring that one new Rentenmark would equal one trillion old paper marks. Nothing physical had changed overnight. The presses had been ordered to stop and a new unit was offered, backed on paper by a mortgage on German land and industry rather than by gold, and enough people agreed to accept it. This chapter lays side by side the people who watched the old agreement die and the people who wrote the new one. The fall is measured in the official record: about 9,000 marks to the dollar in November 1922; around 21,000 through the spring of 1923, when the Reichsbank briefly propped the rate; over a million by the end of July; 160 million by the end of September, after the government ended passive resistance in the Ruhr; and past a trillion on 14 November. Inside those numbers are the dated voices. In Berlin, Käthe Kollwitz's diary records the intellectual middle class being wiped out and a loaf of bread at 140 billion. Betty Scholem, who ran a family printing works, wrote to her son in Jerusalem that postage would double in two days. A man known only as Wolfgang wrote to an American composer that the pensioners in his building were starving. In Dresden, Victor Klemperer watched the price of his wife's coffee double while she drank it. Harry Graf Kessler compared the daily dollar rate to a fever chart. Around them stand the people who saw it from outside or from above. Ernest Hemingway, aged 23, crossed the Rhine from Strasbourg to Kehl in September 1922 and wrote for Toronto readers how ten francs bought a feast, and how an old man could not afford the apples. Lord D'Abernon, the British ambassador, kept a diary in Berlin that he published in 1929. Hjalmar Schacht, appointed currency commissioner on 12 November 1923, wrote his own account in 1927. Two later voices are labelled as later: Erna von Pustau of Hamburg, whose memories Pearl Buck published in 1947, and Edgar Bissantz, an American student who closed his father's Bremen account in 1923 and wrote about it in 1986. The French and Belgian side appears only as context. Their troops entered the Ruhr on 11 January 1923 to enforce reparations deliveries, and the German government answered with paid passive resistance, financed by printing money. No French or Belgian diaries are included here. Other gaps: no industrial worker's or farmer's diary was found in a form that could be verified; Reichsbank president Rudolf Havenstein, who died on 20 November 1923, left official statements but no diary used here; no New York Times dispatch could be reached; and Adam Fergusson's 1975 compilation 'When Money Dies' is not used as a source. Where possible the underlying diaries are cited directly. Much of the record is letters, newspaper dispatches, an economic weekly and official decrees, not diaries, and the form tags say so. title: One City, Two Names for Every Street
eyes: US Consulate General, Jerusalem (Thomas C. Wasson; William Burdett; John J. Macdonald)
United Nations General Assembly, Security Council and Mediator's staff (official record)
places: Christ Church compound, Old City, just inside Jaffa Gate
Consulate General, west Jerusalem, and meetings at the French Consulate
Government offices around the King David Hotel, Jerusalem
His house in Qatamon, west Jerusalem; from 30 April 1948 a refugee in Cairo
Jerusalem, in the guarded zone near the King David Hotel
Jerusalem; visited Deir Yassin on 11 April 1948
Jewish Agency offices, Rehavia, west Jerusalem
Lake Success and Flushing Meadows, New York; Rhodes; Jerusalem
Mediator's headquarters on Rhodes, with repeated visits to Jerusalem
Tel Aviv (reporting a meeting in Jerusalem)
intro: On 29 November 1947 the United Nations General Assembly voted to partition Mandatory Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state, and to set Jerusalem apart from both as a corpus separatum under an international regime. That arrangement for the city never came into force. Within eighteen months Jerusalem was instead cut in two along the lines where the fighting stopped: the New City in the west held by Israel, the Old City and the east held by Transjordan's Arab Legion, with a strip of no man's land, barbed wire and sandbagged houses between them. The records here are set side by side as positions, not as a verdict. Palestinian Arab residents of the western neighbourhoods remember this as the start of the Nakba, the loss of their homes in Qatamon, Talbiyeh and the villages around the city; Jewish residents remember the siege of the New City and the fall of the Old City's Jewish Quarter; British, American, United Nations and Red Cross officials wrote from between the lines. Each community's own records are used for its own experience. Where the records disagree about numbers or responsibility, the chapter reports who said what, and leaves it there. The firsthand record is uneven. Khalil Sakakini's diary and his daughter Hala's dated notes describe Qatamon from inside a house that its family left on 30 April 1948. The Anglican clergyman Hugh Jones kept a journal inside the Old City walls. Sir Henry Gurney, the Mandate's Chief Secretary, kept a diary until the day the administration left. Telegrams from the US Consulate General, printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, give a dated official voice; David Ben-Gurion's diary gives the view from Tel Aviv. Other key accounts were written or published later: Dov Joseph's memoir of governing besieged Jewish Jerusalem (1960), Pablo de Azcárate's UN memoir (1966), Abdullah al-Tall's memoir (1959), and the Red Cross delegate Jacques de Reynier's book (1950), whose 1948 memorandum on Deir Yassin also survives. Harry Levin's siege diary (1950) and Count Folke Bernadotte's diary (1951) are digested here only in outline, because their day-by-day texts could not be checked for this chapter. Gaps are named rather than filled. The Arabic dailies Filastin and al-Difa', published in Jaffa until spring 1948, and the Palestine Post in Jerusalem, whose offices were bombed on the night of 1 February 1948, are cited only as places to read further. The diaries and memoirs of the musician Wasif Jawhariyyeh and of other Old City Arab families, and Hebrew diaries from the Jewish Quarter, exist but are not digested here. Deir Yassin appears only through the Red Cross delegate's own report and the figures each party gave him. Deaths and flight are given soberly and with attribution. title: One Wave Function, Three Readings
places: Princeton, then Arlington/Washington area; Copenhagen in spring 1959; Austin in 1977
Princeton; Chapel Hill in January 1957; Copenhagen in 1959
Princeton; Leiden and Copenhagen in spring 1956; Chapel Hill in January 1957
intro: In 1955 and 1956 a Princeton graduate student, Hugh Everett III, wrote out a proposal that the quantum wave function never collapses. A measuring observer, on this view, does not see one outcome chosen by chance; the observer becomes correlated with every outcome, and each version of the observer has a definite record relative to its own branch. The idea later became famous as 'many worlds', a name Everett himself did not use. This chapter follows the idea as it passed from hand to hand. In Princeton, his adviser John Wheeler admired it and worried about its language. In Copenhagen, where Wheeler carried it in May 1956, Niels Bohr's circle read it as a misunderstanding of what physics is for. At Chapel Hill, North Carolina, home of the January 1957 gravitation conference, Bryce DeWitt first rejected it and later championed it. One text, read in three places, produced three different theories of what it meant. The record is almost entirely letters, drafts and notes, not diaries. Most of it was found in 2007–2009 in a basement belonging to Everett's son, Mark, and is scanned in the UC Irvine 'Hugh Everett III Manuscripts', alongside copies from the Wheeler papers at the American Philosophical Society and the Niels Bohr Archive. Because these are modern and under copyright, everything here is summarised, with links to the scans. Two famous stories, that the idea arrived after a 'slosh or two of sherry' and that the 1959 meeting with Bohr was 'hell', exist only as Everett's recollections in a conversation recorded by Charles Misner in 1977. They are labelled as later accounts. Bohr himself left no known written comment on Everett; his view reaches us only through Wheeler, Petersen and Everett. Nancy Gore, who typed the long thesis and married Everett in 1957, left no firsthand account found for this chapter. Everett left physics for the Pentagon in mid-1956, before the thesis was finished, and never returned. The theory spent the next thirteen years mostly in other people's letters until DeWitt's 1970 Physics Today article made it famous.

title: Barbed Wire Sunday: Berlin Divided Overnight

intro: In the early hours of Sunday 13 August 1961, East German police, soldiers and factory militia unrolled barbed wire along the 43-kilometre line between East and West Berlin and tore up streets at the crossings. Trains and trams stopped at the sector boundary. By breakfast the two halves of a city that had shared underground lines, workplaces and families were cut apart, and over the following days the wire was replaced by concrete blocks and bricked-up house fronts. Two months earlier Walter Ulbricht had told a press conference that no one intended to build a wall. Very little of this chapter's record is diary. The first weeks were written down mostly by institutions: the Stasi's secret reports to the leadership on how the population was reacting, the East Berlin police journal logging crowds and escapes entry by entry, a transport-police report on the first fatal shooting, and on the Western side a mayor's letter, a President's reply, a Vice President's report and a general's telegrams, which the US Foreign Relations series has since published. Around them stand open letters between writers on both sides, newspaper headlines, a photograph, and accounts by survivors' families written down decades later. Each entry is labelled for what it is. The GDR's own position is given in its own documents. The Council of Ministers presented the closure as the ordinary border control of a sovereign state against espionage, the luring away of workers and West German militarism, and the barrier later received the official name 'antifaschistischer Schutzwall'. Stephan Hermlin argued that Berlin had been divided since 1948. The Western positions are given in theirs: Brandt called the closure the most serious encroachment since the blockade and feared a ghetto; Kennedy wrote that only war could reverse it and chose to reinforce West Berlin instead; and the West Berlin press accused the allies of doing nothing. Western rights in West Berlin and Western access were the lines the United States had said it would defend, and those were not crossed. Between the papers are people. Conrad Schumann, a 19-year-old policeman, jumped the wire on the third day. Ida Siekmann, 58, jumped from her window on Bernauer Straße on 22 August and died. Günter Litfin, 24, was shot in the water of the Humboldthafen on 24 August. Neither victim left words of their own, and they appear here only through what others recorded; their deaths are given soberly, as the records give them, and with the gap between the police log's few lines and the newspapers' headlines left visible. Some expected voices are missing. No diary entry by Brigitte Reimann about 13 August 1961 was found in the sources checked; her diary is represented by an earlier entry on her brother's departure to the West. title: The Weekend the Dollar Let Go of Gold
places: Camp David, Maryland, 13–15 August; the White House for the broadcast; the Smithsonian Institution in December
Federal Reserve Bank of New York / Washington
Texas, then Washington and Camp David; Rome in November
The White House (outside the Camp David meeting)
The White House and Camp David
Washington; Camp David; London on 16 August; Rome in November
intro: For twenty-five years the money of the Western world had rested on one promise. Other currencies were pegged to the dollar, and foreign central banks could hand in their dollars at the US Treasury for gold at $35 an ounce. By the summer of 1971 there were far more dollars abroad than gold in Fort Knox, Germany had already let the mark float, and on 12 August over a billion dollars more was pushed onto European central banks. On Friday 13 August, Richard Nixon took about fifteen advisers to Camp David and told them to make no outside calls. The State Department and the National Security Council were not told. On Sunday night he went on television and announced that the dollar would no longer be converted into gold, alongside a wage-price freeze and a 10 percent import surcharge. From then on the dollar was backed by nothing but the willingness of people to keep using it. The record of the weekend is mostly American and official: the address in the Public Papers, the State Department's Foreign Relations volume, and H. R. Haldeman's diary, which he dictated each night and which the Nixon Library has transcribed. Arthur Burns's private diary, published in 2010, gives the dissent. William Safire, Paul Volcker, Charles Coombs and Herbert Stein wrote years later and are labelled so. Abroad, most voices come through US memoranda that recorded them, through Satō Eisaku's diary in Tokyo, and through a Japanese economist's note dated three days after the yen began to float. Some gaps remain. Nothing by Lord Cromer was found on the British request that American memoirs call the final straw, and British papers deny it was ever a request for gold. Pierre-Paul Schweitzer of the IMF appears only through an American memo. Japanese finance officials, Giscard d'Estaing in Paris and the press of Le Monde and Asahi left records that this chapter could not consult directly. Was it necessary? At the time Connally argued that the shock would force surplus countries to revalue, and Shultz, close to Milton Friedman, preferred floating rates in any case. Volcker's later account treats a run on the remaining gold as only days away. Against that, Burns warned of a run on the dollar, retaliation abroad and blame falling on the President, and Europeans and Japanese protested a decision taken without them. Later critics link the end of the gold anchor to the inflation of the 1970s, while defenders say the fixed system could not have survived. The records here show each side's reasoning rather than settle the question. The repair came on 18 December 1971 at the Smithsonian Institution, where new parities were set and the dollar was devalued against gold, though it stayed unconvertible. Nixon called it the most significant monetary agreement in the history of the world. It lasted fourteen months: after a second devaluation in February 1973, the major currencies were floating by March 1973.

title: Private Books: Jung's Black Books and Dick's Exegesis
places: Fullerton (Dick's letter); Disch in New York
Küsnacht, Zürich; travelling to Munich (1913) and Aberdeen (1914); military service at Château-d'Oex (1917)
On a journey (later accounts: by train, towards Schaffhausen)
intro: This chapter sets two private books on one timeline. Between 1913 and 1917 the Swiss psychiatrist C. G. Jung, newly cut off from Freud, recorded a long run of waking visions and inner dialogues in small black notebooks, then rewrote them as an illuminated manuscript he called Liber Novus. Sixty years later, in February and March 1974, the American novelist Philip K. Dick had a cluster of experiences he named '2-3-74' and spent the rest of his life writing about them in an enormous private notebook he called the Exegesis. The two men did not share a century, a language or a profession, and their experiences are not offered here as the same. What they share is a pattern. Each was a professional builder of interpretations who suddenly had an experience he could not interpret. Each wrote it down at once, kept the full record close for the rest of his life, and let out only fragments: Jung a privately printed pamphlet and a small club, Dick long letters to a graduate student and fellow writers. Each book was opened to outside checking only decades after its author's death, in 2009 and 2011. The record is honest only about one side. Jung's dated journals survive and are now published; the people he is said to have confided in, Toni Wolff and Maria Moltzer, left no published firsthand account of these years, and his wife Emma's surviving letters on the subject date from 1911. Dick's letters survive, but the replies of his main correspondents are unpublished, and his wife Tessa's recollections came decades later. Where a person appears here only through someone else's pages, the entry says so. Much of the best-known material is later firsthand. The vision of a flood over Europe is told in Jung's memoir of 1962, written with Aniela Jaffé, and his reading of it as a forecast of the 1914 war is his own later interpretation. The fish sign at Dick's door is told in a speech of 1977 and an essay of 1978, and even its day is disputed. The record ledger at the end of the chapter measures the distance between each event and its first telling. There is also a darker kind of checking. The same Dick who wrote patient letters about dreams wrote to the FBI naming fellow writers and critics as part of hidden schemes. A private world tested against others can become a private world imposed on them. All texts in this chapter are in copyright, so every entry is a summary in plain words, with links to the editions and archives.
